L0: cite0†iframe†www.googletagmanager.com L1: # Introduction to REST API
L2: 
L3: REST API provides you with programmatic access to your data in Salesforce. The flexibility and scalability of REST API make it an excellent choice for integrating Salesforce into your applications and for performing complex operations on a large scale.
L4: Use this guide to set up your deployment environment and learn about advanced details regarding data access. However, understanding and using REST API requires basic familiarity with software development, web services, and the Salesforce user interface.
L5: 
L6: If you want to get right to the action, the Quick Start guide covers the basics to get you up and running.
L7: 
L8: If you’re looking for more context about Salesforce APIs, check out the list of links.
L9: Salesforce REST API is designed to work with Salesforce objects. See the cite1†Object Reference for the Salesforce Platform for an introduction and more information about Salesforce objects.
L10: 
L11:   * cite2†About REST API L12: 
L13: REST API is one of several web interfaces that you can use to access your Salesforce data without using the Salesforce user interface. With API access, you can perform operations and integrate Salesforce into your applications as you like.
L14: 
L15:   * cite3†REST API Release Notes L16: Use the Salesforce Release Notes to learn about the most recent updates and changes to REST API.
L17: 
L18:   * cite4†Supported Editions and Required Permissions L19: 
L20: To access your Salesforce org and data using the Salesforce API, you need both an org and a user with API access enabled. There’s more than one Salesforce Edition that supports API access and multiple ways to grant API permission to a user.
L21: 
L22:   * cite5†REST Resources and Requests L23: REST API is based on the usage of resources—pieces of data in Salesforce, such as records, collections of records, query results, metadata, or API information. Each resource is exposed by a uniform resource identifier (URI) and is accessed by sending HTTP requests to the corresponding URI.
L24: 
L25:   * cite6†REST API Architecture L26: 
L27: REST API follows the standard RESTful principles and characteristics.
L28: 
L29:   * cite7†Authorization Through External Client Apps or Connected Apps and OAuth 2.0 L30: For a client application to access REST API resources, it must be authorized as a safe visitor. To implement this authorization, use either an external client app or a connected app and an OAuth 2.0 authorization flow.
L31: 
L32:   * cite8†Headers L33: 
L34: REST API supports several standard and custom HTTP headers, including both request headers and response headers.
L35: 
L36:   * cite9†Send REST Requests with cURL L37: The examples in this guide use the cURL tool to send HTTP requests that access, create, and manipulate resources in Salesforce. If you use a different tool to send requests, you can use the same elements from the cURL examples to send requests.
L38: 
L39:   * cite10†Valid Date and DateTime Formats L40: 
L41: Specify the right format for `dateTime` and `date` fields.
L42: 
L43:   * cite11†Status Codes and Error Responses L44: 
L45:   * cite12†API End-of-Life Policy L46: 
L47: See which REST API versions are supported, unsupported, or unavailable.
L48: 
L49: See Also
L50:   * cite13†Trailhead: Lightning Platform API Basics†trailhead.salesforce.com --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

L27: # APIs
L28: 
L29: REST and GraphQL APIs generated from your workspace schema.
L30: ##
L31: 
L32: cite3†​ L33: 
L34: Schema-per-tenant APIs
L35: There is no static API reference for Twenty. Each workspace has its own schema — when you add a custom object (say `Invoice`), it immediately gets REST and GraphQL endpoints identical to built-in objects like `Company` or `Person`. The API is generated from the schema, so endpoints use your object and field names directly — no opaque IDs. Your workspace-specific API documentation is available under Settings → API & Webhooks after creating an API key.
L36: It includes an interactive playground where you can execute real calls against your data.
L37: ##
L38: 
L39: cite4†​ L40: 
L41: Two APIs
L42: 
L43: Core API — `/rest/` and `/graphql/` CRUD on records: People, Companies, Opportunities, your custom objects. Query, filter, traverse relations. Metadata API — `/rest/metadata/` and `/metadata/` Schema management: create/modify/delete objects, fields, and relations. This is how you programmatically change your data model. Both are available as REST and GraphQL. GraphQL adds batch upserts and the ability to traverse relations in a single query. Same underlying data either way.
L44: ##
L45: 
L46: cite5†​ L47: 
L48: Base URLs
L49: 
L50: Environment  | Base URL
L51: --- | ---
L52: Cloud  | `https://api.twenty.com/`
L53: Self-Hosted  | `https://{your-domain}/`
L54: ##
L55: 
L56: cite6†​ L57: 
L58: Authentication
L59: 
L60:     `Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY
L61:     `
L62: 
L63: Create an API key in Settings → API & Webhooks → + Create key. Copy it immediately — it’s shown once. Keys can be scoped to a specific role under Settings → Members → Roles → Assignment tab to limit what they can access. For OAuth-based access (external apps acting on behalf of users), see cite9†OAuth .
L64: ##
L65: 
L66: cite7†​ L67: 
L68: Batch operations
L69: 
L70: Both REST and GraphQL support batching up to 60 records per request — create, update, or delete. GraphQL also supports batch upsert (create-or-update in one call) using plural names like `CreateCompanies`.

L72:

L75: Rate limits
L76: 
L77: Limit  | Value
L78: --- | ---
L79: Requests  | 100 per minute
L80: Batch size  | 60 records per call

L2:   * cite0†Home†podio.com L3:   * cite1†Pricing†progress.com L4:   * cite2†What people say†progress.com L5:   * cite3†Blog†progress.com L6:   * cite4†About†progress.com L7:   * cite5†App Market†podio.com L8:   * cite6†Log in†podio.com L9:   * cite7†Getting started L10:   * cite8†Get an API key L11:   * cite9†Authentication L12:     * cite10†Scopes & Permissions L13:     * cite11†Server-side flow L14:     * cite12†Client-side flow L15:     * cite13†Username & password flow L16:     * cite14†App authentication flow L17:   * cite15†API Reference L18:   * cite16†Tutorials L19:   * cite17†Client Libraries L20:   * cite18†Developer Forums†support.sharefile.com L21:   * cite19†Partner Extensions†podio.com L22:   * cite20†Terms of Use†api.sharefile.com L23: # How to authenticate with Podio API
L24: 
L25: The Podio API uses the cite21†OAuth2 protocol†oauth.net for authentication. This allows external apps to request authorization to Podio without having direct access to the user's password. Our API supports different OAuth flows depending on what kind of integration you are making.
L26: Before you can use the Podio API you must cite8†register your application . Your application is assigned a unique identifier, called "Client ID", together with a "Client Secret". You will need both of these to authenticate. The Client Secret should not be shared with anyone.
L27: ### Authentication flows
L28: 
L29: Podio supports four different ways of autheticating depending on what kind of application you are building:
L30: cite11†Server-side flow L31:     This is the preferred way of authenticating for web apps.
L32: cite12†Client-side flow L33:     Use the client-side flow if your application does not have a server. Examples: Browser extensions, web app running purely in the browser, mobile or desktop applications.
L34: cite13†Username & password flow L35:     Use this flow only if none of the other flows are suitable. It requires the user's username and password to be shared.
L36: cite14†App authentication flow L37:     Use app authentication if you only need to interact with a single Podio app and do not need to authenticate as a specific user. Examples: Automated scripts.
L38: All of these authentication methods will provide you with an access token. You will be including this access token in any subsequent requests to the API. You will do this by including an HTTP header with the access token like so:
L39: 
L40: `Authorization: OAuth2 ACCESS_TOKEN`
L41: 
L42: Where ACCESS_TOKEN should be replaced with the actual access token you have obtained. If you are using one of our cite17†client libraries this is handled for you automatically.
L43: ### Token Expiry
L44: 
L45: All tokens received have an associated expiry time. Access Token & refresh Token can be exchanged prior to expiry.
L46: 
L47: ##### Token Expiry Time:
L48: 
L49:   * Access Token: 8 hours
L50:   * Refresh Token: 28 days
L51: 
L52: Recommended Usage:
L53: 
L54:   * By default, the access token is valid for 8 hours. So, you need NOT request a new token with each new API call.
L55:   * App Authentication flow, being more secure, is the preferred way of authentication over Username and Password flow.
L56: ### Refreshing expired tokens
L57: In addition to the access token, the response also contains a expires_in parameter, and a refresh_token parameter. The value of the expires_in parameter is the number of seconds until the token expires. This is an example of a full response when obtaining an access token:
L58: 
L59:     `
L60:     {
L61:       "access_token": ACCESS_TOKEN,
L62:       "token_type": "bearer",
L63:       "expires_in": EXPIRES_IN,
L64:       "refresh_token": REFRESH_TOKEN,
L65:       "scope": GRANTED_SCOPE_STRING,
L66:       "ref":
L67:       {
L68:         "type": "user",
L69:         "id": USER_ID
L70:       }
L71:     }
L72:     `
L73: See cite22†Scopes & Permissions for details about the value of GRANTED_SCOPE_STRING
L74: When the access token expires, you can use the refresh_token to "refresh" your access, and gain another access_token. To use the refresh_token you need to do a POST request to our token-endpoint with the grant_type set to refresh_token:
L75: 
L76:     `
L77:         HTTP METHOD: POST
L78:         URL: https://api.podio.com/oauth/token/v 2
L79:         HEADER:  "Content-Type: application/json"
L80:         BODY:
L81:         {
L82:           "grant_type": "refresh_token",
L83:           "client_id": YOUR_APP_ID,
L84:           "client_secret": YOUR_APP_SECRET,
L85:           "refresh_token": REFRESH_TOKEN,
L86:         }
L87:     `
L88: This request returns the same data as above, and you can continue to do this over and over again, to keep your application authenticated without having to ask the user to re-authenticate.
L89: ### State parameter & Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
L90: 
L91: In order to avoid Cross Site Request Forgery attacks, we recommend you to use an optional state-parameter to pass an identifier, and then validate the state on the response you get from our API.
L92: 
L93: When you make the request to obtain the authorization code include the state parameter like so:
L94: 
L95: `https://podio.com/oauth/authorize?client_id=YOUR_APP_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_URL&state=YOUR_CSRF_TOKEN`
L96: When the Podio API redirects the user back to your application the state parameter is included and you can validate it:
L97: 
L98: ` http://YOUR_URL?code=A_CODE_GENERATED_BY_SERVER&state=YOUR_CSRF_TOKEN `
L99: 
L100: The state parameter is optional. Any string value can be used.
